title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 They Didn't Teach You How To Read
author: Cauthen, Colton
summary: Literacy and reading are not the same thing. Most people are taught to decode symbols into meaning but not to read in the fuller sense, which involves progressive mastery across Mortimer Adler's four levels: Elementary, Inspectional, Analytical, and Syntopical. The article argues that treating reading as a binary skill—you either can or cannot—rather than a developable complex skill causes three predictable harms: people conclude they dislike reading when they are simply not yet skilled enough; they plateau because they believe there is nothing more to develop; and they mistake volume for depth, exemplified by listening to hundreds of books at 2.5x speed and calling it reading. Like chess or surgery, the skill of reading admits degrees of mastery that most people never approach—and most do not realize this. The good news is that recognizing reading as a cultivatable skill reverses all three harms, opening a path toward a richer reading life built through discipline, curiosity, and good practice.
points: * Literacy (decoding symbols) and reading in the full analytical sense are different skills; most people are taught the former and never develop the latter. * Adler's four-level hierarchy—Elementary, Inspectional, Analytical, Syntopical—frames reading as a progressively complex skill at which most people plateau at level one without realizing it. * Treating reading as binary rather than developmental causes people to conclude they dislike it when they are simply not yet skilled enough to experience its rewards. * The volume-hype reading scene—hundreds of books per year at 2.5x speed—mistakes breadth for depth and passive consumption for active, analytical engagement. * Recognizing reading as a cultivatable skill reverses all three harms: reframes frustration as a growth stage, reveals the plateau, and redirects attention from volume to quality.
quotes: One of the biggest misconceptions about reading is that most people know how to do it. The hard truth we need to face if we're going to become intelligent readers is that just because we're literate, doesn't mean we know how to read (in the fullest sense).

Learning to read well is more like learning to play chess than checkers. I have learned how to play chess before— I know the rules of the game, the names of the pieces and what they can do. I cannot, by any means, play chess well.
What we fail to realize is that we just aren't good at it yet, and no one likes doing something they aren't good at unless they can see a light at the end of the tunnel.

Thinking we've achieved all there is to achieve, we just keep reading at our current level. This kind of practice may yield some marginal improvements over time, but like lifting the same weights the same number of times, it will be more maintenance than growth.

I recently overheard someone boasting about how they had read many of the classics one year and now were on to other things. As the conversation unfolded it became evident that what they meant by 'reading' was listening on 2.5+ speed while doing other things.
A rich reading life is not built accidentally or haphazardly. It is cultivated slowly through discipline, curiosity, humility, and good practice.
